name: When Students May Use AI in Science
title: When Students May Use AI in Science
answer: Science and computer science teachers need clear rules about when students may use AI, just as math teachers do. The AI use levels from Chapter 3 work well, and the rules should match the purpose of each task. Students should also disclose how they used AI, so that AI use stays honest and visible.

sections.body: This idea is that science and computer science teachers need clear rules about when students may use AI, just as math teachers do. The AI use levels from Chapter 3 work well for this purpose. The rules should match the purpose of each task, so that the same tool may be allowed in one activity and not in another. This solves the problem of unclear expectations, where students may not know whether AI help is permitted and teachers may not know how tools are being used. It also keeps the focus on what each task is meant to teach.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: In practice, a lab report might allow AI feedback on a draft but not AI writing, while a research project on a science topic might allow AI for finding sources that students then check. A coding exercise that builds basic skills might be marked no AI at all. When the goal is learning to design an experiment, AI should coach but not design. When the goal is learning to debug code, AI should explain errors but not fix them. When the goal is exploring a big data set, AI might be allowed to help with the analysis so students can focus on what the results mean.
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: The text gives no study, figure or finding for this idea, so it rests on practice rather than research. The guidance comes from the book's own account of how the AI use levels from Chapter 3 can be applied to science and computer science tasks. No evidence label is stated in the supplied text.
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: The limits and risks are set by the purpose of each task, and the decisions stay with the teacher. AI should coach but not design when the goal is learning to design an experiment, explain errors but not fix them when the goal is learning to debug code, and help with analysis only when the goal is exploring a big data set so students can focus on what the results mean. Students should disclose how they used AI, with a short note at the end of a lab report or project saying which tool was used and for what. Teachers can use these notes to see how students are using tools and to adjust the rules, and over time disclosure becomes a normal part of how students present their work.
